story: Anthropic's 22 Oct 2026 guide tells builders to try folding specialist subagents back into one agent loop, often faster and cheaper, but it is a conditional 'measure it' recommendation, not a verdict that single agents beat multi-agent setups.
input: Anthropic says single AI agents beat multi-agent setups (Silicon Report archive, week of 19 Oct 2026: https://www.siliconreport.com/ai/archive/2026-10)
verdict_summary: 9 verified, 7 need softer wording (incl. C0 premise), 0 unverified, 1 false (C16, colour only). C0 holds only with qualifiers; all 4 core claims (C0-C3) survive.

claims.text: Anthropic says single AI agents beat multi-agent setups

sources.quote: Anthropic says single AI agents beat multi-agent setups
a single agent with skills frequently outperformed both the one-prompt-for-everything design and the subagent design

claims.safe_text: Anthropic says that in several enterprise deployments, a single agent that loads skills and tools on demand frequently beat a multi-subagent design, often more cheaply and faster, but subagents 'still have their place' and teams should test before folding.

checked_sources.quote: In our comparisons across several enterprise deployments, a single agent with skills frequently outperformed both the one-prompt-for-everything design and the subagent design on quality
To be clear, subagents still have their place, including at the research frontier.
Anthropic says single AI agents beat multi-agent setups
Anthropic says one AI agent beats many subagents now that models can handle complexity alone

claims.note: Judged as worded. Anthropic never says 'single AI agents beat multi-agent setups' as a general rule. As worded, the premise overstates, so it cannot run unqualified. It is not false, though: Anthropic does say a single agent with skills 'frequently outperformed' the subagent design on quality, 'often at a lower cost and latency per task', in its comparisons 'across several enterprise deployments'. The qualifiers that make it true are: 'frequently' (not always); Anthropic's own unpublished comparisons (no figures or method); a single agent *with skills/tools loaded on demand* (not any single agent); and the explicit caveat that subagents still have their place (context bloat, parallel work). Its title is 'When to fold subagents', which is conditional advice. Silicon Report's own body text reports the subagent caveat, which undercuts its headline. Writers must never show the headline wording as Anthropic's claim; they may quote it as the press headline (see C15).

claims.text: In August 2026 Anthropic research found a coordinating agent swarm found 266 vulnerabilities over a 27 million token run, versus 21 for a simple independent parallelized method over 6.5 million tokens.

sources.quote: while the coordinating agent swarm found 266 vulnerabilities over a 27 million token run.
the simple independent parallelized method produces 21 vulnerabilities over a 6.5 million token run

claims.safe_text: In an August 2026 Anthropic experiment, a coordinating agent swarm found 266 vulnerabilities using 27 million tokens, versus 21 for independent parallel agents using 6.5 million tokens; about half the swarm's finds were in code the parallel agents weren't assigned.

checked_sources.quote: For Mythos Preview, the simple independent parallelized method produces 21 vulnerabilities over a 6.5 million token run
while the coordinating agent swarm found 266 vulnerabilities over a 27 million token run.
the two methods seem comparable in terms of tokens per vulnerability found

claims.note: Numbers verbatim; page dated Aug 13, 2026, Frontier Red Team (corresponding author Carolyn Zou). Scope: one experiment with Mythos Preview. Roughly half of the 266 were outside the core directories the independent agents were told to search; within those directories tokens-per-vulnerability were comparable; only 12 overlapped; findings were validated by an arbiter agent, no human verification described. So it is NOT a clean 'swarms find 12x more bugs' result: 01-research.md's '12x more bugs' framing must not be used. The swarm also used ~4x the tokens.

claims.text: A Vals study cited by The Decoder found scaling from ten to 30 or 100 agents brought no quality gains but significantly higher costs (tier 3 only; primary study not opened).

sources.quote: Scaling from ten to 30 or 100 agents brought no quality gains but significantly higher costs, according to the study.

checked_sources.quote: Scaling from ten to 30 or 100 agents brought no quality gains but significantly higher costs, according to the study.
Teams cost 1.8 to 5.1 times as much as single agents, and only one difference in score was statistically significant.

claims.note: The Decoder sentence is quoted correctly, but it is contradicted by the primary source. The Vals study (Vals AI blog, 9 Oct 2026, Katrina Drozdov, Vibe Code Bench) capped teams at five concurrent subagents and did not test 10, 30 or 100 agents. Its actual finding: teams cost 1.8-5.1x as much as single agents and only one score difference (GPT 6 Sol, medium effort) was statistically significant. The 10/30/100 scaling figures appear to come from other, secondary-reported data showing small (not zero) gains. Do not use. If a writer wants the Vals point, it would need a new claim from the Vals primary post and a fresh check.
